But South Carolina would not leave the Union content with these meager trophies of success. The same national Convention that had annulled the tariff law met again and accepted the concession that was offered. At the same time, however, it declared that it held as firmly as ever to the doctrine of Nullification. To prove it, it annulled the law that gave the President extraordinary powers, although it was quite certain that the provisions of that law would never be carried out.

Almost all the disputes I have been describing took place under the presidency of General Jackson, and it cannot be denied that on the tariff question he defended the claims of the Union with vigor and skill. I am nevertheless of the opinion that the conduct of the man who now heads the federal government may be counted among the dangers that threaten its survival.

Some people in Europe have formed an opinion about the influence General Jackson may have on the affairs of his country, and those who have looked more closely into the matter find it highly exaggerated. We have been told that General Jackson has won a number of battles, that he is an energetic man, inclined by nature and by habit to use force, greedy for power, and a despot by temperament. All this may perhaps be true, but the conclusions drawn from it are badly mistaken. People have imagined that General Jackson is determined to establish a dictatorship in America, to introduce a military spirit, and to give the central authority a degree of influence that could not fail to endanger local liberties. But in America the time for such undertakings has not yet come, and neither has the age for men of this kind. If General Jackson had hoped to exercise his authority in this way, he would certainly have lost his political position and put his life at risk. He has accordingly not been so imprudent as to attempt anything of the kind.

Far from wishing to extend federal power, the President belongs to the party that wants to confine it to the bare letter of the Constitution and that never interprets that document in a way favorable to the government of the Union. Far from being a champion of centralization, General Jackson is the instrument of all the jealousies of the States, and the passions of the people that are most hostile to the central government put him in the high office he holds. By constantly flattering those passions he keeps his position and his popularity. General Jackson is the slave of the majority: he yields to its wishes, its inclinations and its demands. Or rather, he anticipates and forestalls them.

Whenever the governments of the States come into conflict with that of the Union, the President is generally the first to doubt his own rights. He almost always goes further than the legislature, and when the extent of federal power is disputed, he takes sides, in a manner of speaking, against himself. He hides his official interests and suppresses his own natural inclinations. This is not because he is naturally weak or hostile to the Union. When the majority ruled against the claims of the supporters of nullification, he put himself at its head, stated the doctrines the nation held clearly and forcefully, and was the first to recommend forceful measures. But General Jackson seems to me, if I may use the American expressions, to be a Federalist by taste and a Republican by calculation.

General Jackson stoops to win the favor of the majority. But once he feels his popularity is secure, he sweeps aside every obstacle in pursuit of the goals the community approves of, or of those it does not view with a jealous eye. He is backed by a power his predecessors never knew, and he tramples on his personal enemies whenever they cross his path with an ease no earlier President ever enjoyed. He takes responsibility for measures that no one before him would have dared to attempt. He even treats the national representatives with a disdain that comes close to insult. He vetoes the laws of Congress, and he often does not bother to answer that powerful body. He is a favorite who sometimes treats his master roughly. The power of General Jackson is constantly growing, but that of the President is declining. In his hands the federal government is strong, but it will pass weakened to his successor.

I am strangely mistaken if the federal government of the United States is not constantly losing strength, gradually withdrawing from public affairs, and narrowing its sphere of action more and more. It is feeble by nature, and now it gives up even the pretense of strength. On the other hand, I thought I noticed in the States a livelier sense of independence and a more decided attachment to local government. The Union is to survive, but only as a shadow. It is to be strong in some cases and weak in all others. In time of war it is to be able to gather the whole strength of the nation and all the resources of the country into its hands, and in time of peace its existence is to be barely noticeable, as if this alternation of weakness and vigor were natural or even possible.

I do not see anything at present that might check this general movement of public opinion, and the causes that gave rise to it continue to operate with the same effect. The change will therefore go on, and it may be predicted that, unless some extraordinary event occurs, the government of the Union will grow weaker every day.

I think, however, that the time is still far off when federal power will be entirely extinguished by its inability to protect itself and to keep the peace in the country. The Union is supported by the customs and the wishes of the people, its results are plain, and its benefits are visible. When people see that the weakness of the federal government endangers the existence of the Union, I have no doubt that a reaction will follow, aimed at increasing its strength.

Of all the federal governments established so far, the government of the United States is the one most naturally destined to act. As long as it is attacked only indirectly, through the interpretation of its laws, and as long as its substance is not seriously altered, a change of opinion, an internal crisis or a war may restore all the vigor it needs. The point I have been most anxious to bring out clearly is simply this. Many people, especially in France, imagine that opinion in the United States is changing in favor of a centralization of power in the hands of the President and Congress. I hold that a contrary tendency can plainly be observed. Far from gaining strength and threatening the sovereignty of the States as it grows older, the federal government is, I maintain, growing weaker and weaker, and it is the sovereignty of the Union alone that is in danger. Such are the facts the present time reveals. The future conceals where this tendency will finally lead, and which events may check, slow or hasten the changes I have described. But I do not pretend to be able to lift the veil that hides them from our sight.
Of the Republican Institutions of the United States, and What Their Chances of Duration Are

The Union is accidental — The republican institutions have better prospects of permanence — A republic is, for the present, the natural state of the Anglo-Americans — Reason for this — To destroy it, all the laws must be changed at the same time, and a great change must take place in customs — Difficulties the Americans experience in creating an aristocracy.

The breakup of the Union might bring war into the heart of the States that are now confederated, along with standing armies, a dictatorship and heavy taxation, and in the end it might endanger the republican institutions. But we ought not to confuse the future prospects of the republic with those of the Union. The Union is an accident that will last only as long as circumstances favor it. A republican form of government, however, seems to me to be the natural state of the Americans, and nothing but the continued action of hostile causes, always working in the same direction, could change it into a monarchy. The Union exists mainly in the law that formed it, and one revolution or one change in public opinion might destroy it forever. But the republic rests on a much deeper foundation.

What is understood by a republican government in the United States is the slow and quiet action of society upon itself. It is an orderly state of things truly founded on the enlightened will of the people. It is a conciliatory government, in which decisions are given time to ripen, are discussed deliberately, and are carried out with mature judgment. Republicans in the United States set a high value on morality, respect religious belief, and acknowledge the existence of rights. They profess to think that a people ought to be moral, religious and temperate in proportion as it is free. What is called the republic in the United States is the tranquil rule of the majority, which, after it has had time to examine itself and to give proof of its existence, is the common source of all the powers of the State. But the power of the majority is not unlimited in itself. In the moral world, humanity, justice and reason enjoy an undisputed supremacy, and in the political world, vested rights are treated with no less deference. The majority recognizes these two barriers. If it now and then oversteps them, it is because it has passions, like individuals, and, like them, is prone to do wrong even while it sees what is right.

But the demagogues of Europe have made strange discoveries. According to them, a republic is not the rule of the majority, as has been thought until now, but the rule of those who are zealous partisans of the majority. It is not the people who predominate in this kind of government, but those who are best versed in the good qualities of the people. This is a happy distinction, which allows men to act in the name of nations without consulting them, and to claim their gratitude while their rights are trampled. A republican government, moreover, is the only kind that claims the right to do whatever it chooses and to despise what men have respected until now, from the highest moral obligations to the ordinary rules of common sense. Until our time it had been supposed that despotism was odious in whatever form it appeared. But it is a discovery of modern days that there is such a thing as legitimate tyranny and holy injustice, provided they are exercised in the name of the people.

The ideas the Americans have adopted about the republican form of government make it easy for them to live under it and ensure that it lasts. If in their country this form is often bad in practice, it is at least good in theory, and in the end the people always act in conformity with it.

It was impossible at the founding of the States, and it would still be difficult today, to establish a central administration in America. The inhabitants are scattered over too wide a space and separated by too many natural obstacles for one man to undertake to direct the details of their lives. America is therefore preeminently the country of local and municipal government. To this cause, which all the Europeans of the New World plainly felt, the Anglo-Americans added several others peculiar to themselves.

When the North American colonies were settled, municipal liberty had already made its way into the laws as well as the customs of the English, and the emigrants adopted it, not only as a necessity but as a benefit whose value they knew. We have already seen how the colonies were founded. Every province, and almost every district, was settled separately by men who were strangers to one another, or who had come together for very different purposes. The English settlers in the United States therefore saw early that they were divided into a great number of small, distinct communities that belonged to no common center. They saw that each of these little communities had to take care of its own affairs, since there seemed to be no central authority that was naturally bound, and easily able, to look after them. Thus the nature of the country, the way the British colonies were founded, the habits of the first emigrants, in short everything, combined to promote municipal and provincial liberties to an extraordinary degree.

In the United States, therefore, the great mass of the country’s institutions is essentially republican. To destroy permanently the laws that form the basis of the republic, it would be necessary to abolish all the laws at once. At the present day it would be even harder for a party to succeed in founding a monarchy in the United States than for a group of men to proclaim that France should from now on be a republic. Royalty would not find a body of legislation prepared for it in advance, and a monarchy would then exist surrounded, in fact, by republican institutions. The monarchical principle would likewise have great difficulty in making its way into the customs of the Americans.

In the United States, the sovereignty of the people is not an isolated doctrine unrelated to the prevailing customs and ideas of the people. On the contrary, it may be regarded as the last link in a chain of opinions that binds the whole Anglo-American world. That Providence has given every human being the degree of reason necessary to direct himself in the affairs that concern him alone is the great maxim on which civil and political society rests in the United States. The father of a family applies it to his children, the master to his servants, the township to its officers, the province to its townships, the State to its provinces, and the Union to the States. When it is extended to the nation, it becomes the doctrine of the sovereignty of the people.

Thus in the United States the fundamental principle of the republic is the same one that governs most human actions. Republican notions work their way into all the ideas, opinions and habits of the Americans, while they are formally recognized by the legislation, and before this legislation can be altered the whole community must undergo very serious changes. In the United States even the religion of most citizens is republican, since it submits the truths of the other world to private judgment, just as in politics the care of temporal interests is left to the good sense of the people. Thus every man is allowed to take freely the road he thinks will lead him to heaven, just as the law gives every citizen the right to choose his government.
It is evident that nothing but a long series of events, all tending the same way, can replace this combination of laws, opinions and customs with a mass of opposite opinions, customs and laws.

If republican principles are to perish in America, they can yield only after a laborious social process, often interrupted and as often resumed. They will have many apparent revivals, and they will not become completely extinct until an entirely new people has replaced the one that now exists. Now, it must be admitted that there is no symptom or sign that such a revolution is approaching. Nothing is more striking to a person newly arrived in the United States than the kind of tumultuous agitation in which he finds political society. The laws change incessantly, and at first sight it seems impossible that a people so changeable in its desires could avoid adopting a completely new form of government within a short time. Such fears are, however, premature. The instability that affects political institutions is of two kinds, which ought not to be confused. The first kind, which modifies secondary laws, is not incompatible with a very settled state of society. The other shakes the very foundations of the Constitution and attacks the fundamental principles of legislation. This kind of instability is always followed by troubles and revolutions, and the nation that suffers from it is in a state of violent transition.

Experience shows that the two kinds of legislative instability are not necessarily linked, since they have appeared together or separately depending on the time and the circumstances. The first is common in the United States, but the second is not. The Americans change their laws often, yet the foundation of the Constitution is respected.

Today the republican principle rules in America as the monarchical principle ruled in France under Louis XIV. The French of that time did not merely favor the monarchy; they could not imagine anything taking its place. They took it for granted, as we take the sun’s rays and the return of the seasons. Royal power had neither defenders nor opponents among them. In the same way, republican government exists in America without dispute or opposition, without proofs or arguments, by a tacit agreement, a sort of consensus universalis. Even so, it is my opinion that by changing their administrative forms as often as they do, the inhabitants of the United States put the future stability of their government at risk.

It may be feared that men, constantly thwarted in their plans by the changeability of the legislation, will come to regard republican institutions as an inconvenient form of society. The harm resulting from the instability of the secondary enactments might then raise a doubt about the nature of the fundamental principles of the Constitution and indirectly bring about a revolution. But that time is still very remote.

It may, however, be foreseen even now that when the Americans lose their republican institutions, they will quickly arrive at a despotic government, without a long interval of limited monarchy. Montesquieu remarked that nothing is more absolute than the authority of a prince who immediately succeeds a republic, since the powers that had been entrusted without fear to an elected magistrate are then transferred to a hereditary sovereign. This is true in general, but it applies more particularly to a democratic republic. In the United States the magistrates are not elected by a particular class of citizens but by the majority of the nation. They are the immediate representatives of the passions of the multitude, and since they depend wholly on its pleasure, they inspire neither hatred nor fear. Hence, as I have already shown, very little care has been taken to limit their influence, and they are left in possession of a vast amount of arbitrary power. This state of things has produced habits that would outlive it: the American magistrate would keep his power but would cease to be responsible for how he uses it, and it is impossible to say what limits could then be set to tyranny.

Some of our European politicians expect to see an aristocracy arise in America, and they already predict the exact time at which it will be able to take the reins of government. I have observed before, and I repeat, that the present tendency of American society appears to me to be toward ever greater democracy. I do not claim, nevertheless, that the Americans will never, at some future time, narrow the circle of political rights in their country, or confiscate those rights for the benefit of a single individual. But I cannot imagine that they will ever give the exclusive exercise of those rights to a privileged class of citizens, or, in other words, that they will ever found an aristocracy.

An aristocratic body consists of a certain number of citizens who, though not very far removed from the mass of the people, stand permanently above it. It is a body that is easy to touch and hard to strike. The people are in daily contact with it, yet can never unite with it. Nothing is more contrary to nature and to the secret leanings of the human heart than this kind of subjection, and men left to their own inclinations will always prefer the arbitrary power of a king to the regular administration of an aristocracy. Aristocratic institutions cannot last unless they make the inequality of men a fundamental principle, built into the legislation and affecting the condition of the human family as much as that of society. But such things are so repugnant to natural equity that they can be wrung from men only by force.

I do not think a single people can be cited, since human society began, that has by its own free will and its own exertions created an aristocracy within itself. All the aristocracies of the Middle Ages were founded by military conquest: the conqueror was the noble, and the conquered became the serf. Inequality was then imposed by force, and once it had been introduced into the customs of the country it sustained its own authority and was sanctioned by the legislation. There have been communities that were aristocratic from their earliest origin, owing to circumstances that preceded it, and that became more democratic with each succeeding age. Such was the fate of the Romans, and of the barbarians after them. But a people that began in civilization and democracy and that gradually established an inequality of conditions, until it arrived at inviolable privileges and exclusive castes, would be a novelty in the world, and nothing suggests that America is likely to furnish so singular an example.
Reflection on the Causes of the Commercial Prosperity of the United States

The Americans destined by Nature to be a great maritime people — Extent of their coasts — Depth of their ports — Size of their rivers — The commercial superiority of the Anglo-Americans, however, is less attributable to physical circumstances than to moral and intellectual causes — Reason for this opinion — Future destiny of the Anglo-Americans as a commercial nation — The dissolution of the Union would not check the maritime vigor of the States — Reason for this — The Anglo-Americans will naturally supply the needs of the inhabitants of South America — They will become, like the English, the commercial agents of a great part of the world.

The coastline of the United States runs more than two thousand miles, from the Bay of Fundy to the Sabine River in the Gulf of Mexico. These shores form one unbroken line, all under a single government. No nation in the world has larger, deeper or safer harbors for shipping than the Americans.

The inhabitants of the United States are a great civilized people whom fortune has placed in the midst of an uncultivated country, three thousand miles from the central point of civilization. America consequently needs European trade every day. The Americans will no doubt eventually succeed in producing or manufacturing at home most of the articles they require. But the two continents can never be independent of each other, so numerous are the natural ties between their needs, their ideas, their habits and their customs.

The Union produces distinctive commodities that have now become necessary to us but that cannot be grown in the soil of Europe, or can be raised there only at enormous expense. The Americans consume only a small portion of this produce, and they are willing to sell us the rest. Europe is therefore the market of America, as America is the market of Europe. Maritime commerce is no less necessary to enable the inhabitants of the United States to carry their raw materials to the ports of Europe than it is to enable us to supply them with our manufactured goods. The United States was therefore bound to face an alternative. If it had refused to enter into commerce itself, as the Spaniards of Mexico have so far done, it would have greatly increased the business of other maritime nations. The other course was to become one of the first trading powers of the globe.

The Anglo-Americans have always had a marked taste for the sea. The Declaration of Independence broke the commercial restrictions that bound them to England and gave a fresh, powerful boost to their maritime genius. Since then, the Union’s shipping has grown at nearly the same rapid pace as its population. Today the Americans themselves carry nine-tenths of the European goods they consume to their own shores. *g They also carry three-quarters of the New World’s exports to the European consumer. *h American ships fill the docks of Havre and Liverpool, while English and French vessels are comparatively few at New York. *i

g [ The total value of goods imported during the year that ended on September 30, 1832, was $101,129,266. The value of the cargoes of foreign vessels did not amount to $10,731,039, or about one-tenth of the entire sum.]

h [ The value of goods exported during the same year amounted to $87,176,943. The value of goods exported by foreign vessels amounted to $21,036,183, or about one quarter of the whole sum. (Williams’s “Register,” 1833, p. 398.)]

i [ The tonnage of the vessels that entered all the ports of the Union in the years 1829, 1830, and 1831, amounted to 3,307,719 tons, of which 544,571 tons were foreign vessels. They stood, therefore, to the American vessels in a ratio of about 16 to 100. (“National Calendar,” 1833, p. 304.) The tonnage of the English vessels that entered the ports of London, Liverpool, and Hull, in the years 1820, 1826, and 1831, amounted to 443,800 tons. The foreign vessels that entered the same ports during the same years amounted to 159,431 tons. The ratio between them was, therefore, about 36 to 100. (“Companion to the Almanac,” 1834, p. 169.) In the year 1832 the ratio between the foreign and British ships that entered the ports of Great Britain was 29 to 100. [These statements relate to a condition of affairs which has ceased to exist; the Civil War and the heavy taxation of the United States entirely altered the trade and navigation of the country.]]

Thus the American merchant not only faces the competition of his own countrymen but also withstands that of foreign nations successfully in their own ports. This is readily explained by the fact that the vessels of the United States can cross the seas more cheaply than any other vessels in the world. As long as American merchant shipping keeps this superiority, it will not only hold on to what it has gained but will steadily grow more prosperous.

It is hard to say why the Americans can trade at a lower rate than other nations, and at first one is led to attribute this to physical or natural advantages within their reach. But that supposition is mistaken. American vessels cost almost as much to build as our own. *j They are not better built, and they generally last a shorter time. The pay of the American sailor is higher than the pay on board European ships, as is proved by the great number of Europeans to be found in the merchant vessels of the United States. But I am of the opinion that the true cause of their superiority must not be sought in physical advantages, and that it is wholly attributable to their moral and intellectual qualities.
j [ Materials are, generally speaking, less expensive in America than in Europe, but the price of labor is much higher.]

The following comparison will illustrate my meaning. During the campaigns of the Revolution, the French introduced a new system of tactics into the art of war, which bewildered the oldest generals and very nearly destroyed the most ancient monarchies in Europe. They undertook, as had never been attempted before, to do without a number of things that had always been held indispensable in warfare. They demanded new exertions from their troops, such as no civilized nation had ever thought of. They achieved great things in an incredibly short time, and they risked human life without hesitation to gain the object in view. The French had less money and fewer men than their enemies, and their resources were infinitely inferior. Nevertheless they were constantly victorious, until their adversaries chose to imitate their example.

The Americans have introduced a similar system into their commercial ventures, and they do for cheapness what the French did for conquest. The European sailor navigates with caution. He sets sail only when the weather is favorable. If an unforeseen accident befalls him, he puts into port. At night he furls part of his canvas, and when the whitening waves signal that land is near, he slows down and takes a reading of the sun. But the American neglects these precautions and braves these dangers. He weighs anchor in the midst of raging gales. By night and by day he spreads his sails to the wind. He repairs as he goes along whatever damage his vessel has suffered from the storm, and when he finally nears the end of his voyage, he darts on toward the shore as if he already saw a port. The Americans are often shipwrecked, but no trader crosses the seas as fast. And since they cover the same distance in a shorter time, they can do it at a lower cost.

The European stops several times at different ports in the course of a long voyage. He loses a good deal of precious time getting into harbor, or waiting for a favorable wind to leave it, and he pays daily dues for the right to remain there. The American sets out from Boston to buy tea in China. He arrives at Canton, stays a few days, and then returns. In less than two years he has sailed the entire circumference of the globe, and he has seen land only once. It is true that during a voyage of eight or ten months he has drunk brackish water and lived on salt meat, and that he has been in constant struggle with the sea, with disease and with the tedium of his existence. But on his return he can sell a pound of his tea for a halfpenny less than the English merchant, and his purpose is accomplished.

The best way I can explain my meaning is to say that the Americans bring a kind of heroism to the way they trade. The European merchant will always find it very hard to imitate his American rival. In following the system I have just described, the American is guided not only by a calculation of profit but by an impulse of his nature.

The inhabitants of the United States are subject to all the wants and desires that come with an advanced stage of civilization. But they are not surrounded, as Europeans are, by a community admirably equipped to satisfy those wants, and so they are often obliged to provide for themselves the various articles that education and habit have made necessities. In America it sometimes happens that the same person tills his field, builds his house, makes his tools, makes his shoes, and weaves the coarse cloth of which his clothing is made. This circumstance is harmful to the quality of the work, but it greatly helps to awaken the intelligence of the worker. Nothing tends more than an extreme division of labor to turn a man into a mere material thing and to strip his work of the faintest trace of mind. In a country like America, where men devoted to special occupations are rare, a long apprenticeship cannot be required of anyone who takes up a profession. The Americans therefore change their means of earning a living very readily, and they suit their occupations to the demands of the moment, in the way most profitable to themselves. One meets men who have been, in turn, lawyers, farmers, merchants, ministers of the gospel and physicians. If the American is less perfect in each craft than the European, there is at least scarcely any trade of which he is completely ignorant. His capacity is more general, and the range of his intelligence is wider.

The inhabitants of the United States are never bound by the axioms of their profession. They escape all the prejudices of their present station. They are no more attached to one line of work than to another, and no more inclined to use an old method than a new one. They have no deep-rooted habits, and they easily shake off the influence that the habits of other nations might have on their minds, out of a conviction that their country is unlike any other and that its situation has no precedent in the world. America is a land of wonders, in which everything is in constant motion and every movement seems an improvement. The idea of novelty is there inseparably connected with the idea of improvement. No natural boundary seems to be set to the efforts of man, and what is not yet done is only what he has not yet attempted to do.

This perpetual change that goes on in the United States, these frequent reversals of fortune, along with such unforeseen fluctuations in private and public wealth, keep the minds of the citizens in a constant state of feverish agitation. This admirably invigorates their efforts and keeps them in a state of excitement above the ordinary level of mankind. The whole life of an American is passed like a game of chance, a revolutionary crisis or a battle. Since the same causes are continually at work throughout the country, they ultimately give the national character an irresistible impulse. The American, taken as a random sample of his countrymen, must then be a man of unusual warmth in his desires, enterprising, fond of adventure, and above all fond of innovation. The same bent shows in everything he does. He brings it into his political laws, his religious doctrines, his theories of social economy and his domestic occupations. He carries it with him into the depths of the backwoods as well as into the business of the city. It is this same passion, applied to maritime commerce, that makes him the cheapest and the quickest trader in the world.

So long as American sailors keep these invigorating advantages and the practical superiority that comes from them, they will go on supplying the needs of the producers and consumers of their own country. They will also tend more and more to become, like the English, the commercial agents of every other people. *k This prediction has already begun to come true. We can see American traders making themselves intermediaries in the commerce of several European nations, *l and America will offer their enterprise a still wider field.

k [ It must not be supposed that English vessels are used only to bring foreign produce into England or to carry British produce abroad. Today English merchant shipping may be regarded as a vast system of public transport, ready to serve all the producers of the world and to open communications between all peoples. The maritime genius of the Americans leads them to compete with the English.]
l [ Part of the commerce of the Mediterranean is already carried on by American vessels.]

The great colonies founded in South America by the Spaniards and the Portuguese have since become empires. Civil war and oppression now lay waste those vast regions. The population does not increase, and the thinly scattered inhabitants are too absorbed in the cares of self-defense even to attempt any improvement of their condition. This, however, will not always be so. Europe has succeeded by her own efforts in piercing the gloom of the Middle Ages. South America has the same Christian laws and Christian customs as we have. She contains all the seeds of civilization that have grown among the nations of Europe or their offshoots, together with the advantages to be gained from our example. Why then should she always remain uncivilized? It is clear that the question is simply one of time. At some future period, more or less remote, the inhabitants of South America will form flourishing and enlightened nations.

But when the Spaniards and Portuguese of South America begin to feel the wants common to all civilized nations, they will still be unable to satisfy those wants for themselves. As the youngest children of civilization, they must of necessity admit the superiority of their elder brethren. They will be farmers long before they succeed in manufacturing or commerce, and they will need strangers to act as intermediaries in exchanging their produce overseas for the articles for which a demand will begin to be felt.
